- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

1	\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
2	
3	Self-consistency (majority voting over multiple samples) yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning \citep{wang2023selfconsistency}, and test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
4	But named entity recognition (NER) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a \textit{set} of entities, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.
5	
6	Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) with \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
7	Existing self-consistency methods \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence, an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
8	Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we provide the first systematic empirical characterization of \textit{when and why} LP-based selection succeeds or fails for structured prediction, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.
9	Our experiments use fine-tuned models, the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER, and separate quality estimation from best-of-$N$ selection.
10	
11	A key distinction structures our analysis: four of five signals (Soft Jaccard, voting confidence, Fleiss' $\kappa$, exact match) are instance-level aggregates that assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; only log-probability (LP) is natively per-sample.
12	All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82; Figure~\ref{fig:overview}), supporting selective prediction.
13	For selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) in settings where both low instance degeneracy and adequate alignment are present, with gains scaling with $N$.
14	On SciERC, the observed LP gain ($+0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$) falls below the minimum detectable effect (${\approx}$1.5~pp at 80\% power, $n{=}529$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom. We term this disparity between quality estimation strength and selection effectiveness the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
15	Three factors qualitatively shape this gap: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy} (13\textendash 87\% across our benchmarks) compresses the candidate space; (b)~\textit{oracle headroom} bounds the achievable gain; (c)~\textit{LP-quality alignment} (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) determines whether LP can discriminate candidates in non-degenerate instances (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
16	Our diagnosis is complementary to minimum Bayes risk (MBR) utility misalignment \cite{eikema2025structured}: where MBR failures in structured prediction stem from poorly chosen utility functions, we find that degeneracy eliminates candidate diversity before utility alignment matters.
17	Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates positively with F1 ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
18	Both mechanisms intensify with model capability: degeneracy rises with scale and training convergence (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). This creates a tension between model quality and test-time improvability.
19	
20	\begin{figure*}[t]
21	\centering
22	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
23	\caption{Overview of the correlation-selection gap and its mitigation. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals reliably estimate instance-level quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}). \textbf{Center}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all samples from the same input, so best-of-$N$ selection cannot outperform greedy. \textbf{Right}: entity-level construction aggregates entities across samples via majority vote ($\theta{=}2/N$), bypassing the selection bottleneck ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD, multi-seed mean; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).}
24	\label{fig:overview}
25	\end{figure*}
26	
27	We evaluate five signals from three families (structural, surface, and model-internal) on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc} as a primary medium-difficulty test bed, with Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (low-degeneracy contrast), CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (ceiling-effect control), and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (signal-collapse boundary), using two 8B models (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with a 4B ablation (Qwen3-4B).
28	We vary candidate pool size ($N{\in}\{2,\ldots,32\}$), signal sophistication, and model capacity across 4B\textendash 8B fine-tuned and 72B zero-shot regimes.
29	An exploratory extension to relation extraction is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
30	Our contributions:
31	\begin{enumerate}
32	    \item \textbf{Quality estimation framework and selective prediction.}
33	    Five signals from three families evaluated on four NER benchmarks, two model families, and a 4B ablation, achieving reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82).
34	    QE enables selective prediction: filtering low-confidence instances at 80\% coverage yields $+5$--$8$\,pp F1 (area under the precision-recall curve [AUPRC] 0.70--0.92, VC strongest; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
35	
36	    \item \textbf{Diagnostic of the correlation-selection gap.}
37	    For fine-tuned 4B--8B models, LP-quality alignment (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) is the primary predictor of selection success: LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) where alignment is strong, but not on benchmarks with weak alignment.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Self-consistency (majority voting over multiple samples) yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning \citep{wang2023selfconsistency}, and test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
But named entity recognition (NER) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a \textit{set} of entities, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) with \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
Existing self-consistency methods \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence, an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we provide the first systematic empirical characterization of \textit{when and why} LP-based selection succeeds or fails for structured prediction, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.
Our experiments use fine-tuned models, the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER, and separate quality estimation from best-of-$N$ selection.

A key distinction structures our analysis: four of five signals (Soft Jaccard, voting confidence, Fleiss' $\kappa$, exact match) are instance-level aggregates that assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; only log-probability (LP) is natively per-sample.
All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82; Figure~\ref{fig:overview}), supporting selective prediction.
For selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) in settings where both low instance degeneracy and adequate alignment are present, with gains scaling with $N$.
On SciERC, the observed LP gain ($+0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$) falls below the minimum detectable effect (${\approx}$1.5~pp at 80\% power, $n{=}529$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom. We term this disparity between quality estimation strength and selection effectiveness the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
Three factors qualitatively shape this gap: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy} (13\textendash 87\% across our benchmarks) compresses the candidate space; (b)~\textit{oracle headroom} bounds the achievable gain; (c)~\textit{LP-quality alignment} (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) determines whether LP can discriminate candidates in non-degenerate instances (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
Our diagnosis is complementary to minimum Bayes risk (MBR) utility misalignment \cite{eikema2025structured}: where MBR failures in structured prediction stem from poorly chosen utility functions, we find that degeneracy eliminates candidate diversity before utility alignment matters.
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates positively with F1 ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Both mechanisms intensify with model capability: degeneracy rises with scale and training convergence (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). This creates a tension between model quality and test-time improvability.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{Overview of the correlation-selection gap and its mitigation. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals reliably estimate instance-level quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}). \textbf{Center}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all samples from the same input, so best-of-$N$ selection cannot outperform greedy. \textbf{Right}: entity-level construction aggregates entities across samples via majority vote ($\theta{=}2/N$), bypassing the selection bottleneck ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD, multi-seed mean; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We evaluate five signals from three families (structural, surface, and model-internal) on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc} as a primary medium-difficulty test bed, with Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (low-degeneracy contrast), CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (ceiling-effect control), and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (signal-collapse boundary), using two 8B models (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with a 4B ablation (Qwen3-4B).
We vary candidate pool size ($N{\in}\{2,\ldots,32\}$), signal sophistication, and model capacity across 4B\textendash 8B fine-tuned and 72B zero-shot regimes.
An exploratory extension to relation extraction is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Quality estimation framework and selective prediction.}
    Five signals from three families evaluated on four NER benchmarks, two model families, and a 4B ablation, achieving reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82).
    QE enables selective prediction: filtering low-confidence instances at 80\% coverage yields $+5$--$8$\,pp F1 (area under the precision-recall curve [AUPRC] 0.70--0.92, VC strongest; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).

    \item \textbf{Diagnostic of the correlation-selection gap.}
    For fine-tuned 4B--8B models, LP-quality alignment (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) is the primary predictor of selection success: LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) where alignment is strong, but not on benchmarks with weak alignment.
    Instance degeneracy causally modulates LP within fixed settings (epoch and temperature ablations), but does not predict cross-dataset direction ($\rho{=}0.052$, 23 configurations); structural signals fail by construction; supervised combinations and hidden state probes (Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}) confirm the gap persists.

    \item \textbf{Entity-level construction as a diagnostic-motivated mitigation.}
    The diagnostic naturally motivates entity-level aggregation, adapting entity voting from ensemble NER \cite{florian2003named} to stochastic sampling: LP-weighted construction yields $+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD and $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC (multi-seed mean, $p{<}0.005$; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
    Construction and LP selection are complementary on two informative datasets, governed by LP-quality alignment; a simple alignment-based gating protocol correctly routes datasets.
\end{enumerate}

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	\paragraph{Datasets.}
8	We evaluate on four English NER benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient, each serving a distinct role.
9	\textbf{SciERC} \cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test instances, 6 entity types) is the primary medium-difficulty test bed where models achieve ${\approx}$65\% F1.
10	\textbf{Few-NERD} \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (INTRA coarse; 37{,}648 instances, 8 entity types, ${\approx}$75\% F1) provides a low-degeneracy contrast where LP selection succeeds (\S\ref{sec:fewnerd}).
11	\textbf{CoNLL-2003} \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (3{,}453 test sentences, 4 entity types, ${\approx}$91\% F1) serves as a ceiling-effect control where limited oracle headroom constrains selection gains.
12	\textbf{WNUT-17} \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (1{,}287 social media instances, 51\% zero F1) probes the signal-collapse boundary where model capability is insufficient.
13	
14	\paragraph{Models and sampling.}

19	\subsection{Quality Estimation Results}
20	\label{sec:qe_results}

44	
45	\paragraph{Signal rankings are difficulty-dependent.}
46	On SciERC (medium difficulty), structural signals lead (VC $\rho{=}0.379$, SJ $0.360$) over LP ($0.205$); bootstrap CIs confirm the gap ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.155$; Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_signal}).
47	On CoNLL (single-sample F1${\approx}$0.91), EM leads both $\rho$ and AUROC ($0.816$).
48	At the signal-collapse boundary (WNUT-17, macro F1${\approx}$42\%), full-set correlations are dominated by the zero/non-zero boundary (VC $\rho{=}0.724$ but conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}); LP shows the reverse (conditional $\rho{=}0.350$; Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}).
49	This collapse illustrates a regime where model capability is insufficient to produce meaningful inter-sample variation: 51\% of instances yield zero F1 across all samples, and consistency signals merely detect this floor rather than discriminating quality among non-trivial outputs.

51	%% ============================================================
52	\subsection{The Correlation-Selection Gap}
53	\label{sec:selection_gap}
54	
55	Four of five signals (SJ, FK, EM, VC) assign identical scores to all candidates from the same input by construction (\S\ref{sec:formulation}); they can estimate quality across instances but cannot rank candidates within an instance.
56	The empirical question is whether LP, the sole per-sample signal, can exploit its candidate-discriminative nature for selection.
57	LP selection effectiveness is primarily determined by LP-quality alignment rather than degeneracy level (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
58	Cross-instance $\rho$ (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}) is attenuated by varying instance difficulty; within-instance $\rho$ directly measures whether LP discriminates candidates for a fixed input, making it the relevant predictor of selection success.
59

61	\centering
62	\small
63	\caption{Best-of-$N$ NER selection (macro F1) on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, 2-seed mean${\pm}\sigma$). LP is per-sample; others use consensus-proximity. Best non-oracle in \textbf{bold}. Non-tied subset in \S\ref{sec:discussion}; RE in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}. $^\dagger$Instance-level signals assign one score per input; per-sample ranking $p$-values are undefined.}

67	Method & NER F1 & $p$ \\

Despite $\rho$ up to 0.38, no signal significantly outperforms greedy (all $p{>}0.05$; Table~\ref{tab:selection}). Dashed green: oracle upper bound ($+13.1$~pp); dotted gray: random baseline.}
90	\label{fig:selection_gap}
91	\end{figure}
92	
93	Instance-level signals assign identical QE scores to all candidates; MBR conversion does not improve over greedy on the primary test bed (Table~\ref{tab:selection}; Figure~\ref{fig:selection_gap}).
94	Instance-level signals predict \textit{which inputs} the model handles reliably, not \textit{which output} is best.
95	
96	\paragraph{LP: the sole per-sample signal also fails.}
97	On SciERC ($n{=}529$, 2-seed sign tests\footnote{MDE${\approx}$1.5~pp at 80\% power ($n{=}529$); Few-NERD ($n{=}32{,}565$; MDE${\approx}$0.22~pp) provides the definitive test.}), the oracle (0.775) reveals 13.0~pp of headroom, but LP achieves $+0.2$~pp ($p{=}0.29$), below the MDE (${\approx}$1.5~pp); selection effects below this threshold cannot be reliably detected.
98	The pattern holds across CoNLL and WNUT-17 (Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}); under stringent TOST anchors, some configurations show significant \textit{degradation} (Appendix~\ref{app:tost}).
99	Few-NERD provides the definitive contrast: LP achieves $+1.39$~pp ($p{<}0.001$) at low degeneracy (\S\ref{sec:fewnerd}), while structural signals still degrade selection.
100	
101	\paragraph{Qualitative factors governing selection effectiveness.}
102	Three factors qualitatively shape LP selection gains: (1)~\textit{instance degeneracy} compresses the candidate space, leaving fewer instances where any signal can improve over greedy (SciERC 17.8\%, CoNLL 61.7\%; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}); (2)~\textit{oracle headroom} bounds the maximum achievable gain (CoNLL ${\approx}2$\,pp vs.\ SciERC 13.1\,pp); (3)~\textit{LP-quality alignment}, measured as within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$, determines whether LP can discriminate candidates in the remaining non-degenerate instances (Few-NERD $\rho{\approx}0.5$--$0.7$ vs.\ SciERC $\rho{\approx}0.26$).
103	These factors are consistent with the observed pattern (Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}): Few-NERD (low degeneracy, strong alignment) shows the largest LP gain ($+1.39$\,pp), SciERC (weak alignment) shows unreliable gains ($+0.04{\pm}0.48$\,pp, 3-seed; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}), CoNLL (high degeneracy, minimal headroom) shows no gain, and WNUT-17 represents the signal-collapse boundary: LP $\rho{=}{-}0.446$ (the model assigns higher log-probabilities to confidently wrong outputs), within-instance alignment absent ($\rho{=}0.043$, n.s.), and construction ineffective ($p{>}0.05$, mixed sign) because 51\% of instances yield F1${=}0$.
104	Yet QE remains effective on WNUT-17 (VC $\rho{=}0.724$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}), confirming QE-selection decoupling at this boundary.
105	This characterization is qualitative: the three factors do not combine into a predictive model ($R^2{<}0$ across 23 configurations), but each factor's role is individually supported by controlled ablations (\S\ref{sec:fewnerd}, \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
106

LP is 50$\times$ more seed-stable ($\sigma{=}0.04$ vs.\ SJ $2.02$~pp) and generalizes to LLaMA-3.1-8B (Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).

132	\paragraph{Degeneracy alone does not predict LP selection direction.}

148	
149	Consistency signals are robust across $T{\in}\{0.7, 1.0\}$ with sublinear $N$-scaling gains (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}); signal rankings are stable across seeds ($W{=}1.0$; Table~\ref{tab:ranking-stability}). NER calibration is reasonable (ECE 0.069--0.096; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}).

168	\paragraph{Scale robustness.}
169	With Qwen3-4B (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}), QE is comparable (mean $|\Delta\rho|{=}0.042$), yet selection remains below greedy despite 13.0~pp headroom. Task difficulty is a stronger predictor than model scale within the 3B--8B range (Appendix~\ref{app:llama3b}).

180	\subsection{Scaling Behavior}
181	\label{sec:scaling}
182	
183	We evaluate Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct in a zero-shot setting to test whether the gap persists at larger scale without fine-tuning.
184

186	\centering

207	LP $\rho$ drops sharply without fine-tuning across all three datasets (Table~\ref{tab:scale_comparison}), and LP selection fails on all. Structural signals generalize to zero-shot (Few-NERD VC $\rho{=}0.416$, SJ $0.345$). Degeneracy increases (Few-NERD: $46.2$\% vs.\ $13.0$\%; CoNLL: $67.7$\% vs.\ $61.7$\%).

Majority vote also succeeds ($+1.39$\,pp); LP-weighting adds $+0.14$\,pp. Construction fails on Few-NERD 72B ZS ($-0.20$\,pp) and CoNLL ($-0.37$\,pp), where degeneracy exceeds $46$\%---consistent with the degeneracy-gating pattern in the fine-tuned regime ($n{=}3$ datasets).

211	%% ============================================================
212	\subsection{Prescriptive Results}
213	\label{sec:prescriptive}
214	
215	The preceding sections establish that instance-level selection fails for structured IE. We now present two approaches that extract value from multi-sample generation without relying on sample ranking.
216	
217	\paragraph{Entity-level construction.}
218	Rather than selecting one of $N$ complete outputs, we aggregate entities across all samples, retaining those exceeding a confirmation threshold $\theta{=}2/N$ (${\geq}2$ of $N$ samples), with LP-weighted or uniform frequency scoring. Under fine-tuning, this default achieves the best or near-best F1 across all datasets ($\theta$ stable within $[0.15, 0.35]$; Appendix~\ref{app:theta_sweep}). In the zero-shot regime, uniform voting degrades (SciERC $-0.52$\,pp, CoNLL $-0.92$\,pp) because greater output diversity admits noise entities; LP-weighting is necessary for construction to succeed without fine-tuning (SciERC $+1.5$\,pp; \S\ref{sec:scaling}).

221	\centering
222	\small

224	\label{tab:entity_construction}
225	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
226	\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccc@{}}
227	\toprule
228	Dataset & Wt. & Greedy & Constr. & $\Delta$ & $p$ \\
229	\midrule
230	SciERC & LP & $.646{\pm}.002$ & $\mathbf{.656{\pm}.003}$ & $+1.02{\pm}0.49$\,pp & .004 \\
231	       & Unif. & $.646{\pm}.002$ & $.653{\pm}.006$ & $+0.74{\pm}0.71$\,pp & .023 \\
232	\addlinespace
233	Few-NERD & LP & $.748$ & $\mathbf{.762{\pm}.005}$ & $+1.40{\pm}0.51$\,pp & ${<}.001$ \\
234	         & Unif. & $.748$ & $.756{\pm}.006$ & $+0.74{\pm}0.58$\,pp & .003 \\
235	\addlinespace
236	CoNLL$^\ddagger$ & Unif. & .908 & .904 & $-0.39$\,pp & n.s. \\
237	\bottomrule
238	\end{tabular}}
239	\end{table}
240	
241	LP-weighted construction improves over greedy on Few-NERD ($+1.40{\pm}0.51$\,pp, $p{<}0.001$) and SciERC ($+1.02{\pm}0.49$\,pp, $p{=}0.004$; Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}), positive across all 7 seed-dataset combinations, recovering ${\approx}$8\% (SciERC) and 11\% (Few-NERD) of oracle headroom. CoNLL shows no gain ($-0.39$\,pp), consistent with ceiling-regime degeneracy. The mechanism is recall-driven: aggregating low-frequency correct entities recovers mentions that no single sample captures ($N$-scaling in Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
242	
243	\paragraph{LP-alignment gating (preliminary diagnostic).}
244	Construction and LP selection are complementary: construction dominates on SciERC ($+1.02$\,pp vs.\ LP $+0.04{\pm}0.48$\,pp, n.s.; $\rho{\approx}0.2$), while on Few-NERD both yield comparable gains ($+1.40$ vs.\ $+1.39$\,pp; $\rho{\approx}0.5$--$0.7$).
245	We estimate within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ on 50 held-out instances with bootstrap CIs (1000 resamples). Degeneracy-adjusted $\rho_{\text{adj}}$: Few-NERD $0.516$ [0.459, 0.759], SciERC $0.167$ [0.146, 0.281], CoNLL $0.065$ [$-$0.061, 0.620], WNUT-17 ${\approx}0$ (n.s.).
246	The protocol performs three-way routing: (1)~$\rho_{\text{adj}} \geq \tau{=}0.3$: apply LP selection; (2)~$\rho_{\text{adj}} < \tau$ and construction shows positive dev-set gain: apply construction; (3)~otherwise: retain greedy decoding.
247	This routes Few-NERD to LP selection ($+1.39$\,pp); SciERC, CoNLL, and WNUT-17 fall below $\tau$ and route to greedy. The conservative protocol trades SciERC's missed construction gain ($+1.02$\,pp) for protection against negative outcomes (CoNLL $-0.39$\,pp, WNUT-17 n.s.).
248	Routing is stable across $\tau{\in}[0.2, 0.4]$ and matches test-set direction for all four datasets; narrower inter-dataset margins remain untested.
249	
250	\paragraph{Selective prediction.}
251	Orthogonal to construction, QE signals support selective prediction: at 80\% coverage, filtering low-confidence instances yields $+5$--$8$\,pp F1 (AUPRC 0.70--0.92; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
252

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; effective selection likely requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}.
Three factors qualitatively constrain selection: instance degeneracy (17.8--67.9\%) compresses the candidate space, limited oracle headroom bounds achievable gains, and LP compression (within-instance $\rho$ 0.043--0.667) prevents exploiting the remainder; within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates positively with F1 (SJ median $\rho{=}0.524$) \cite{eikema2022sampling}.
Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP selection yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}), but $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ is post-hoc ($p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.14$ after joint correction; Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}), so this is exploratory evidence.
Temperature disentangles degeneracy from alignment: at $T{=}1.2$, degeneracy drops to 14.9\% yet LP does not improve (median $\rho{=}0.225$; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}); the selection window narrows as models improve \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, snell2025scaling}.

\paragraph{From diagnosis to practice.}\label{sec:selection_method}
Entity-level construction bypasses both failure mechanisms (Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}), complementary with LP selection and governed by LP-quality alignment (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}). Construction generalizes to zero-shot 72B where degeneracy is low (SciERC: $+1.53$\,pp, recovering $10.2$\% of headroom; FT SciERC: $7.8$\%; FT Few-NERD: $11.3$\%), but fails at high degeneracy (${\geq}46$\%).
Alternative strategies (DALS, MBR, DGS) fail to reliably beat greedy (Appendix~\ref{app:dals}); our negative results are specific to fine-tuned models with constrained decoding (Appendix~\ref{app:when_selection_works}).

140	\paragraph{Per-relation diagnostic.}
141	RE signal degradation is relation-specific.

146	\paragraph{Capability stratification.}
147	For NER, SJ effectiveness scales with structural complexity: on SciERC instances with 6+ entities, $\rho{=}0.547$, compared to $\rho{=}0.415$ for 1--2 entities.
148	The SJ advantage over LP remains stable across sentence-length quartiles ($\Delta\rho{\approx}0.08$--$0.20$).

165	\paragraph{Evaluation circularity and LOO-SJ equivalence.}
166	Consensus-proximity selection chooses $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
167	Leave-one-out SJ (LOO-SJ) for sample $y_i$ is $\text{LOO-SJ}_i = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
168	Since the $\frac{1}{N-1}$ constant is shared across all candidates within an instance, $\arg\max_{y_i} \text{LOO-SJ}_i = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$; the two selection rules are equivalent.
169	Standard (non-LOO) SJ adds the self-comparison term $\text{SJ}(y_i, y_i) = 1$ to each candidate, which is constant and thus does not affect ranking.
170	Empirically, LOO-SJ yields $\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.014$ relative to standard SJ (a correlation-level difference), with a maximum per-instance score difference of $3.1{\times}10^{-4}$ (negligible at the individual prediction level).
171	Evaluation circularity is negligible.

253	\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
254	Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2025scaling}.
255	For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.047$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
256	Structural signals use $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, each additional comparison yields diminishing information.
257	This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ LP $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.163$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while LP does not.
258	For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound (more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate), but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.
259	The practical implication is that $N{=}8$ captures most of the achievable quality estimation benefit; further scaling widens rather than closes the correlation-selection gap absent stronger per-sample selectors.
260	
261	\paragraph{$N{=}16$ CoNLL selection: small but significant.}
262	While quality estimation benefits sublinearly from $N$-scaling, selection behavior at $N{=}16$ reveals a nuanced exception on LLaMA CoNLL.
263	VC achieves the largest gain over single-sample ($+0.28$~pp, $p{=}0.003$--$0.027$ across 3 seeds, all significant), with SJ, FK, and EM at $+0.22$--$0.23$~pp and LP at $+0.12$~pp (2/3 seeds significant).
264	These gains are statistically significant but practically minimal: oracle headroom at $N{=}16$ is only 2.5~pp, so VC captures approximately 10\% of the available headroom.
265	This reinforces the primary finding: even under the most favorable conditions (high baseline performance, more candidates, and aggregated multi-seed evidence), signal-based selection recovers only a fraction of the oracle headroom available.

369	\paragraph{TOST equivalence testing.}\label{app:tost}
370	The primary evidence against selection gains comes from effect sizes and confidence intervals: Cohen's $d{=}0.038$ for the best signal (NER LP) and bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$3.0, $+$4.2]~pp spanning zero.

375	The breakpoint $\delta^*$, the minimum equivalence margin at which each signal passes TOST, ranges from approximately 1.3~pp (SJ, ${\sim}$10\% of oracle headroom) to 3.4~pp (FK, ${\sim}$26\%) on NER, and from approximately 2.9~pp (LP, ${\sim}$16\%) to 6.5~pp (VC, ${\sim}$36\%) on RE.

400	\paragraph{External equivalence margins.}
401	The oracle-headroom anchors above introduce circularity: $\delta$ is calibrated against the very quantity it contextualizes.
402	To resolve this, we supplement with three externally grounded margins:
403	(1) $\delta_{\mathrm{SEM}}$: the bootstrapped standard error of single-sample F1 (0.43--1.33~pp depending on configuration), which represents measurement noise;
404	(2) $\delta_{\mathrm{practical}}{=}0.5$~pp, the threshold below which NER differences are considered negligible \cite{ratinov2009design};
405	(3) $\delta_{\mathrm{literature}}{=}1.0$~pp, the approximate significant-difference threshold established in NER evaluation methodology \cite{bergkirkpatrick2012empirical}.
406	
407	Results under these external anchors diverge sharply by configuration.
408	On LLaMA CoNLL ($n{=}2{,}756$), all signals pass equivalence at every $\delta$ ($p{<}0.001$), consistent with the near-zero selection deltas ($|\Delta|{\leq}0.1$~pp) and tight CIs at this sample size.
409	On Qwen CoNLL ($n{=}2{,}756$), no signal passes at any external $\delta$: selection F1 degrades by 0.9--1.5~pp relative to single-sample, which exceeds even $\delta_{\mathrm{literature}}$.
410	On SciERC NER ($n{=}529$), only SJ passes at $\delta_{\mathrm{SEM}}{=}1.33$~pp (the widest SEM bound); all other signals and tighter margins fail.
411	These external anchors confirm that the equivalence conclusion is configuration-dependent: LLaMA CoNLL selection is robustly equivalent to single-sample under any reasonable margin, while SciERC and Qwen CoNLL selection shows detectable degradation at externally calibrated thresholds.
412	
413	\paragraph{Multiple comparison considerations.}\label{app:multiple_comparisons}
414	Our primary selection analysis involves ${\sim}$20 comparisons (5 signals $\times$ 3--4 configurations).
415	Since all primary selection results are non-significant ($p{>}0.05$), applying Benjamini-Hochberg correction can only make these results more conservative, strengthening the ``no signal beats greedy'' conclusion.
416	The sole positive finding, the non-tied LP subset ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.004$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}), survives Bonferroni correction over the 5 signal comparisons ($p_{\mathrm{adj}}{=}0.020 < 0.05$). However, the $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold is selected post-hoc from a 7-point sweep (Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}); joint correction across thresholds and signals yields $p_{\mathrm{adj}}{=}0.14$, so this finding is exploratory.
417	For quality estimation signal rankings, differences between the top signals (e.g., VC vs.\ SJ on SciERC) should be interpreted as descriptive rather than as statistically confirmed orderings, given the limited power of 3-seed comparisons.
418	
419	\paragraph{When would consistency-based selection work?}\label{app:when_selection_works}
420	Our negative results are specific to fine-tuned models with constrained decoding on structured IE. Several conditions outside our experimental scope could restore selection headroom.
421	(a)~Models with poor calibration or in-context learning setups (without fine-tuning) produce more diverse outputs, widening the gap between candidates that consistency signals can exploit.
422	(b)~Closed-source APIs where log-probabilities are unavailable make consistency signals the only viable selection mechanism; our structural signals (SJ, VC, FK, EM) provide quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45) even without model-internal access.
423	(c)~Ensemble or mixture-of-experts settings generate structurally diverse candidates by design, reducing instance degeneracy below the levels observed in our single-model sampling.
424	(d)~Tasks where the model exhibits systematic overconfidence (e.g., hallucination-prone generation) may benefit from consensus filtering, as disagreement among samples would carry more discriminative signal than in our well-calibrated fine-tuned regime.

428	\subsection{Supervised Signal Combination}
429	
430	Supervised classifiers (logistic regression, MLP, random forest) trained on all five signals (5-fold CV, 3-seed mean, SciERC, $N{=}16$, $+17.9$~pp headroom) all perform at or below greedy (F1${=}0.644$; LR: $-0.4$~pp; MLP: $-1.6$~pp; RF: $-3.1$~pp).
431	Adding pairwise interaction features does not help (AUROC 0.634 vs.\ 0.638).
432	To test whether richer representations could close the gap, we train a DeBERTa-v3-base verifier that encodes input-output pairs and predicts per-sample F1.
433	DeBERTa achieves $\rho{=}0.329{\pm}0.087$ (5-fold CV, 3 seeds). Despite moderate quality prediction, selection utility is poor: on SciERC, DeBERTa closes $-26.5{\pm}26.5$\% of the oracle gap (13 of 15 runs negative; vs.\ LP's $+4.2{\pm}10.7$\%); on Few-NERD, DeBERTa recovers only $+3.5$\% (single 80/20 split; vs.\ LP's $+16.3$\%).
434	Cross-dataset transfer fails entirely ($-27$\% to $-72$\% gap closure).
435	Neither handcrafted signal combinations nor learned text representations close the selection gap; only model-internal log-probability provides meaningful selection signal, consistent with an information asymmetry between the generating model and external observers.

\paragraph{Temperature sensitivity.}
SJ NER $\rho$ shifts from 0.364 ($T{=}0.7$) to 0.360 ($T{=}1.0$), a difference of 0.004.
FK NER $\rho$ drops by 0.022, while RE $\rho$ increases by 0.091, likely reflecting reduced diversity at lower temperature interacting differently across tasks.
LP exhibits the largest temperature effect on NER ($\rho{=}0.249$ at $T{=}0.7$ vs.\ $0.205$ at $T{=}1.0$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.044$), consistent with lower temperature concentrating probability mass and improving LP's discriminative power for quality estimation; RE $T{=}0.7$ LP data is not available.
Across all comparisons, the signal hierarchy is preserved at both temperatures on NER (SJ${>}$FK${>}$LP at $T{=}0.7$: $0.364{>}0.289{>}0.249$; at $T{=}1.0$: $0.360{>}0.267{>}0.205$).

\paragraph{Sample size scaling.}
Increasing from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$ improves SJ on Qwen SciERC NER: $\rho$ rises from 0.360 to $0.411{\pm}0.010$ (three seeds: 0.398, 0.423, 0.410), a gain of $+0.047$.
The magnitude of $N$-scaling gains is setting-dependent (LLaMA SciERC NER yields $+0.016$ and Qwen CoNLL NER $+0.014$), though the direction is consistently positive.
LLaMA CoNLL exhibits the most uniform scaling: all four consistency signals gain $\Delta\rho{\approx}{+}0.042$ (range: $+0.039$ to $+0.044$) while LP gains only $+0.004$ (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}).
FK $N$-scaling is seed-dependent: Qwen SciERC gains range from $+0.005$ to $+0.023$ across seeds (mean $+0.016$), while LLaMA CoNLL yields $+0.039$ (3-seed mean); individual seed FK shifts vary substantially under the unified pipeline, so this should not be interpreted as a robust trend.
VC $N$-scaling is consistently positive ($+0.005$ on Qwen CoNLL, $+0.018$ on LLaMA SciERC, $+0.030$ on Qwen SciERC), while LP is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta{\leq}0.034$).
SJ, EM, and VC scale consistently across all tested settings; only FK shows seed-dependent variation that does not constitute a reliable trend, structural and binary-agreement signals are the most robust to $N$.
At $N{=}16$, SJ converges to comparable NER performance with VC ($\Delta{=}0.002$) while exhibiting lower cross-seed variance ($\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\ $0.026$), a more stable alternative at higher sample sizes.

\paragraph{Transfer across model families.}

\paragraph{Per-relation diagnostic.}
RE signal degradation is relation-specific.
\textsc{Feature-Of} has near-zero correlation ($\rho{=}0.004$), while \textsc{Hyponym-Of} achieves $\rho{=}0.646$.
The primary bottleneck is entity span errors, which account for 55.5\% of RE false negatives. This is a prerequisite failure that consistency signals cannot detect, as they measure agreement among equally incorrect extractions.
We note that RE analysis relies on a single dataset (SciERC); generalization to other RE benchmarks remains to be validated.

\paragraph{Capability stratification.}
For NER, SJ effectiveness scales with structural complexity: on SciERC instances with 6+ entities, $\rho{=}0.547$, compared to $\rho{=}0.415$ for 1--2 entities.
The SJ advantage over LP remains stable across sentence-length quartiles ($\Delta\rho{\approx}0.08$--$0.20$).
For RE, SJ $\rho$ increases monotonically with sentence length (Q1: 0.110 $\to$ Q4: 0.473; Fisher $z$-test $p{=}0.004$): longer, more relation-dense sentences provide richer structure for consistency-based estimation.
Both proxies are weakly correlated with F1 ($|r|{<}0.15$), they capture input complexity rather than directly predicting output quality; however, entity count and sentence length are themselves moderately correlated ($\rho{=}0.650$), so they reflect overlapping rather than independent complexity dimensions.
For RE, entity count and relation count are strongly correlated ($\rho{=}0.769$) and thus reflect a single structural complexity dimension rather than independent axes.
On the high-complexity RE subset ($n{=}81$, high relation count), signals improve substantially: VC reaches $\rho{=}0.630$, LP $\rho{=}0.554$, and SJ $\rho{=}0.502$, all far above the full-set levels.
Richer relational structure provides more signal for consistency-based estimation, complementing the task-level boundary established by WNUT-17: structural signals are most effective within a ``sweet spot'' of sufficient model capability and sufficient output complexity.

\paragraph{Evaluation circularity and LOO-SJ equivalence.}
Consensus-proximity selection chooses $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
Leave-one-out SJ (LOO-SJ) for sample $y_i$ is $\text{LOO-SJ}_i = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
Since the $\frac{1}{N-1}$ constant is shared across all candidates within an instance, $\arg\max_{y_i} \text{LOO-SJ}_i = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$; the two selection rules are equivalent.
Standard (non-LOO) SJ adds the self-comparison term $\text{SJ}(y_i, y_i) = 1$ to each candidate, which is constant and thus does not affect ranking.
Empirically, LOO-SJ yields $\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.014$ relative to standard SJ (a correlation-level difference), with a maximum per-instance score difference of $3.1{\times}10^{-4}$ (negligible at the individual prediction level).
Evaluation circularity is negligible.

\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2025scaling}.
For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.047$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
Structural signals use $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, each additional comparison yields diminishing information.
This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ LP $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.163$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while LP does not.
For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound (more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate), but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.
The practical implication is that $N{=}8$ captures most of the achievable quality estimation benefit; further scaling widens rather than closes the correlation-selection gap absent stronger per-sample selectors.

\paragraph{$N{=}16$ CoNLL selection: small but significant.}
While quality estimation benefits sublinearly from $N$-scaling, selection behavior at $N{=}16$ reveals a nuanced exception on LLaMA CoNLL.
VC achieves the largest gain over single-sample ($+0.28$~pp, $p{=}0.003$--$0.027$ across 3 seeds, all significant), with SJ, FK, and EM at $+0.22$--$0.23$~pp and LP at $+0.12$~pp (2/3 seeds significant).
These gains are statistically significant but practically minimal: oracle headroom at $N{=}16$ is only 2.5~pp, so VC captures approximately 10\% of the available headroom.
This reinforces the primary finding: even under the most favorable conditions (high baseline performance, more candidates, and aggregated multi-seed evidence), signal-based selection recovers only a fraction of the oracle headroom available.

\paragraph{TOST equivalence testing.}\label{app:tost}
The primary evidence against selection gains comes from effect sizes and confidence intervals: Cohen's $d{=}0.038$ for the best signal (NER LP) and bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$3.0, $+$4.2]~pp spanning zero.
Table~\ref{tab:tost} supplements this with two one-sided tests (TOST), testing whether each signal's selection F1 is equivalent to single-sample within a bound $\delta$.
The $\delta$ values are contextualized against oracle headroom (12--18~pp): $\delta{=}5$~pp corresponds to forgoing 28--38\% of the available headroom, $\delta{=}3$~pp forgoing 17--23\%, and $\delta{=}2$~pp less than 15\%.
These proportions use the same test data that defines the headroom, introducing circularity: $\delta$ is anchored to the very quantity it contextualizes.
We address this below with externally anchored equivalence margins.
The breakpoint $\delta^*$, the minimum equivalence margin at which each signal passes TOST, ranges from approximately 1.3~pp (SJ, ${\sim}$10\% of oracle headroom) to 3.4~pp (FK, ${\sim}$26\%) on NER, and from approximately 2.9~pp (LP, ${\sim}$16\%) to 6.5~pp (VC, ${\sim}$36\%) on RE.
On NER ($n{=}529$), at $\delta{=}{\pm}2$~pp, SJ and LP are confirmed equivalent to single-sample (TOST $p{<}0.05$); at $\delta{=}{\pm}3$~pp, four of five signals pass; at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp, all five pass.
On RE ($n{=}397$, preliminary), EM and VC fail equivalence even at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp due to systematic underperformance ($\Delta{=}{-}3.2$~pp and $-4.5$~pp respectively).
The effect sizes are negligible ($d{=}0.038$) and confidence intervals span zero, with TOST confirming equivalence at practically meaningful margins.

\paragraph{External equivalence margins.}
The oracle-headroom anchors above introduce circularity: $\delta$ is calibrated against the very quantity it contextualizes.
To resolve this, we supplement with three externally grounded margins:
(1) $\delta_{\mathrm{SEM}}$: the bootstrapped standard error of single-sample F1 (0.43--1.33~pp depending on configuration), which represents measurement noise;
(2) $\delta_{\mathrm{practical}}{=}0.5$~pp, the threshold below which NER differences are considered negligible \cite{ratinov2009design};
(3) $\delta_{\mathrm{literature}}{=}1.0$~pp, the approximate significant-difference threshold established in NER evaluation methodology \cite{bergkirkpatrick2012empirical}.

Results under these external anchors diverge sharply by configuration.
On LLaMA CoNLL ($n{=}2{,}756$), all signals pass equivalence at every $\delta$ ($p{<}0.001$), consistent with the near-zero selection deltas ($|\Delta|{\leq}0.1$~pp) and tight CIs at this sample size.
On Qwen CoNLL ($n{=}2{,}756$), no signal passes at any external $\delta$: selection F1 degrades by 0.9--1.5~pp relative to single-sample, which exceeds even $\delta_{\mathrm{literature}}$.
On SciERC NER ($n{=}529$), only SJ passes at $\delta_{\mathrm{SEM}}{=}1.33$~pp (the widest SEM bound); all other signals and tighter margins fail.
These external anchors confirm that the equivalence conclusion is configuration-dependent: LLaMA CoNLL selection is robustly equivalent to single-sample under any reasonable margin, while SciERC and Qwen CoNLL selection shows detectable degradation at externally calibrated thresholds.

\paragraph{Multiple comparison considerations.}\label{app:multiple_comparisons}
Our primary selection analysis involves ${\sim}$20 comparisons (5 signals $\times$ 3--4 configurations).
Since all primary selection results are non-significant ($p{>}0.05$), applying Benjamini-Hochberg correction can only make these results more conservative, strengthening the ``no signal beats greedy'' conclusion.
The sole positive finding, the non-tied LP subset ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.004$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}), survives Bonferroni correction over the 5 signal comparisons ($p_{\mathrm{adj}}{=}0.020 < 0.05$). However, the $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold is selected post-hoc from a 7-point sweep (Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}); joint correction across thresholds and signals yields $p_{\mathrm{adj}}{=}0.14$, so this finding is exploratory.
For quality estimation signal rankings, differences between the top signals (e.g., VC vs.\ SJ on SciERC) should be interpreted as descriptive rather than as statistically confirmed orderings, given the limited power of 3-seed comparisons.

\paragraph{When would consistency-based selection work?}\label{app:when_selection_works}
Our negative results are specific to fine-tuned models with constrained decoding on structured IE. Several conditions outside our experimental scope could restore selection headroom.
(a)~Models with poor calibration or in-context learning setups (without fine-tuning) produce more diverse outputs, widening the gap between candidates that consistency signals can exploit.
(b)~Closed-source APIs where log-probabilities are unavailable make consistency signals the only viable selection mechanism; our structural signals (SJ, VC, FK, EM) provide quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45) even without model-internal access.
(c)~Ensemble or mixture-of-experts settings generate structurally diverse candidates by design, reducing instance degeneracy below the levels observed in our single-model sampling.
(d)~Tasks where the model exhibits systematic overconfidence (e.g., hallucination-prone generation) may benefit from consensus filtering, as disagreement among samples would carry more discriminative signal than in our well-calibrated fine-tuned regime.

\section{Supervised and Model-Internal Signal Analysis}\label{app:supervised_combination}

\subsection{Supervised Signal Combination}

Supervised classifiers (logistic regression, MLP, random forest) trained on all five signals (5-fold CV, 3-seed mean, SciERC, $N{=}16$, $+17.9$~pp headroom) all perform at or below greedy (F1${=}0.644$; LR: $-0.4$~pp; MLP: $-1.6$~pp; RF: $-3.1$~pp).
Adding pairwise interaction features does not help (AUROC 0.634 vs.\ 0.638).
To test whether richer representations could close the gap, we train a DeBERTa-v3-base verifier that encodes input-output pairs and predicts per-sample F1.
DeBERTa achieves $\rho{=}0.329{\pm}0.087$ (5-fold CV, 3 seeds). Despite moderate quality prediction, selection utility is poor: on SciERC, DeBERTa closes $-26.5{\pm}26.5$\% of the oracle gap (13 of 15 runs negative; vs.\ LP's $+4.2{\pm}10.7$\%); on Few-NERD, DeBERTa recovers only $+3.5$\% (single 80/20 split; vs.\ LP's $+16.3$\%).
Cross-dataset transfer fails entirely ($-27$\% to $-72$\% gap closure).
Neither handcrafted signal combinations nor learned text representations close the selection gap; only model-internal log-probability provides meaningful selection signal, consistent with an information asymmetry between the generating model and external observers.

\subsection{Hidden State Probes}\label{app:hidden_probe}

The preceding negative results suggest the bottleneck is model-internal rather than a feature engineering problem.
We test this directly by training probes on the generating model's hidden representations.

\paragraph{Setup.}
For each of $N{=}8$ samples per instance, we extract the mean-pooled final-layer hidden state ($d{=}4096$) from the generating Qwen3-8B model and train a linear probe and a two-layer MLP (hidden dim${=}256$) to predict per-sample F1 (5-fold CV, 3 seeds).

\paragraph{Cross-dataset asymmetry.}
On SciERC, the MLP probe achieves higher quality correlation than LP ($\rho{=}0.388$ vs.\ $0.283$, $+37$\%); hidden states encode information beyond what LP captures.
Yet higher correlation does not yield better selection: MLP selection F1 ($0.637$) falls below LP's ($0.650$), with gap closure turning negative ($-5.1$\% vs.\ $+4.8$\%; Table~\ref{tab:hidden_probe}).
The linear probe performs worse still ($\rho{=}0.179$, gap closure $-23.4$\%).
On Few-NERD, the MLP provides no increment over LP (gap closure $11.7$\% vs.\ $12.3$\%).
A learned token-level LP aggregator (1D CNN over per-token log-probabilities) matches mean LP on Few-NERD (gap closure $56.4$\% vs.\ $55.8$\%); LP's bottleneck is not token aggregation.
The correlation-selection gap extends to model-internal representations: in the high-capability regime (greedy F1${=}0.644$), inter-sample F1 differences are small enough that improved ranking provides no marginal selection value, consistent with the capability-diversity tension (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

539	\paragraph{Prompt template.}
540	For NER, we use a structured prompt:
541	\begin{quote}
542	\small
543	\texttt{System:} You are an expert in Named Entity Recognition.\\
544	\texttt{User:} Extract all named entities from the following text. Output as JSON.\\
545	Text: \texttt{\{input\_text\}}\\
546	Entity types: \texttt{\{schema\_types\}}
547	\end{quote}
548	RE follows the same structure with ``Relation Extraction'' and relation type lists substituted accordingly.
549	
550	\paragraph{Constrained decoding.}
551	Inference uses vLLM with XGrammar-based JSON schema enforcement \cite{dong2024xgrammar, willard2023guided}, which constrains outputs to valid entity/relation structures matching the target schema.
552	This eliminates format errors but may compress per-sample diversity by restricting the output space.\footnote{SciERC training used \texttt{enable\_thinking=True} (LLaMA Factory 0.9.4 default), injecting empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks (4--5 tokens) into each training response with loss computation; CoNLL and WNUT explicitly set \texttt{enable\_thinking=False}. Constrained decoding at inference time enforces JSON-only output, suppressing thinking tokens. See \S\ref{sec:setup} and Limitations for discussion of this confound.}
553	
554	\section{Thinking Token Impact Analysis}\label{app:thinking_token}
555	
556	Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint was trained with empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks prepended to each response (\S\ref{sec:setup}).
557	We quantify the potential impact on LP scores through three complementary arguments.
558	
559	\paragraph{LP shift magnitude.}
560	Empty thinking tokens (mean 4.5 per sample) constitute 2.1\% of tokens on SciERC.
561	The estimated LP shift is 0.001 nats per token (2.68\% of the median within-instance LP range of 0.041 nats).
562	Because all samples share identical thinking-token LP offsets, cumulative LP rankings are invariant; mean LP changes selection for ${<}1.5\%$ of instances.
563	
564	\paragraph{Constant prefix cancellation.}
565	All $N$ samples within an instance share the same prompt and, under constrained decoding, the same absence of thinking tokens at inference time.
566	Any LP bias from the training-time thinking prefix is therefore a near-constant additive shift across all candidates within an instance, leaving within-instance LP \textit{rankings} unchanged.
567	
568	\paragraph{CoNLL control group.}
569	CoNLL and WNUT-17 checkpoints were trained without thinking tokens (\texttt{enable\_thinking=False}).
570	If thinking tokens caused LP compression on SciERC, CoNLL should exhibit lower tied fractions.
571	Instead, CoNLL shows \textit{higher} tied fractions at both temperatures (86.8\% at $T{=}1.0$, 95.8\% at $T{=}0.7$) than SciERC (60.3\% at $T{=}1.0$), directly contradicting the thinking-token hypothesis.
572	
573	\section{Log-Probability Score Compression}\label{app:logprob_ties}
574	
575	Under constrained decoding, log-probability scores are severely compressed within instances, limiting per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}, Figure~\ref{fig:lp_range_cdf}).
576	The median within-instance LP range is only 0.041 nats; we use $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ as an illustrative threshold to characterize this compression.
577	At this cutpoint, 60.3\% of instances ($n{=}529$, excluding empty gold annotations) have a within-sample range below $\varepsilon$, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\Delta|{<}0.026$).
578	The CDF rises smoothly with no cliff or discontinuity (Figure~\ref{fig:lp_range_cdf}); compression is a pervasive regime rather than a bimodal split.
579	This compression is stable across seeds: seed${=}456$ yields median LP range${=}0.040$ nats and tied fraction${=}62.2\%$ (vs.\ seed${=}42$: $0.041$ nats, $60.3\%$).
580	Seed~456 uses a different subtask flag (joint vs.\ ner for seeds 42 and 123); the LP distributions are statistically indistinguishable (median LP: 8.37 vs.\ 8.20 nats; Mann--Whitney $p{=}0.55$); the subtask change does not affect compression.
581	For comparison, SJ has only 12.5\% tied instances at the same threshold; SJ's advantage over LP for selection is one of score resolution, not information content.

826	\section{MBR Decoding and Task-Specific Interactions}\label{app:mbr_discussion}
827	
828	\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
829	Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
830	Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here: despite positive within-instance utility--F1 correlation, selection gains are limited by instance degeneracy, the core of the correlation-selection gap.
831	\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs, consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.
832	
833	\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
834	The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
835	On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
836	The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
837	This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
838	This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); whether the RE reversal replicates across seeds and generalizes to other RE benchmarks warrants further investigation.
839	The non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472: 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, and the newly non-tied subset shows a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.
840	Despite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible. Score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.
841	Free-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\rho$: 0.379$\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.

\paragraph{Prompt template.}
For NER, we use a structured prompt:
\begin{quote}
\small
\texttt{System:} You are an expert in Named Entity Recognition.\\
\texttt{User:} Extract all named entities from the following text. Output as JSON.\\
Text: \texttt{\{input\_text\}}\\
Entity types: \texttt{\{schema\_types\}}
\end{quote}
RE follows the same structure with ``Relation Extraction'' and relation type lists substituted accordingly.

\paragraph{Constrained decoding.}
Inference uses vLLM with XGrammar-based JSON schema enforcement \cite{dong2024xgrammar, willard2023guided}, which constrains outputs to valid entity/relation structures matching the target schema.
This eliminates format errors but may compress per-sample diversity by restricting the output space.\footnote{SciERC training used \texttt{enable\_thinking=True} (LLaMA Factory 0.9.4 default), injecting empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks (4--5 tokens) into each training response with loss computation; CoNLL and WNUT explicitly set \texttt{enable\_thinking=False}. Constrained decoding at inference time enforces JSON-only output, suppressing thinking tokens. See \S\ref{sec:setup} and Limitations for discussion of this confound.}

\section{Thinking Token Impact Analysis}\label{app:thinking_token}

Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint was trained with empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks prepended to each response (\S\ref{sec:setup}).
We quantify the potential impact on LP scores through three complementary arguments.

\paragraph{LP shift magnitude.}
Empty thinking tokens (mean 4.5 per sample) constitute 2.1\% of tokens on SciERC.
The estimated LP shift is 0.001 nats per token (2.68\% of the median within-instance LP range of 0.041 nats).
Because all samples share identical thinking-token LP offsets, cumulative LP rankings are invariant; mean LP changes selection for ${<}1.5\%$ of instances.

\paragraph{Constant prefix cancellation.}
All $N$ samples within an instance share the same prompt and, under constrained decoding, the same absence of thinking tokens at inference time.
Any LP bias from the training-time thinking prefix is therefore a near-constant additive shift across all candidates within an instance, leaving within-instance LP \textit{rankings} unchanged.

\paragraph{CoNLL control group.}
CoNLL and WNUT-17 checkpoints were trained without thinking tokens (\texttt{enable\_thinking=False}).
If thinking tokens caused LP compression on SciERC, CoNLL should exhibit lower tied fractions.
Instead, CoNLL shows \textit{higher} tied fractions at both temperatures (86.8\% at $T{=}1.0$, 95.8\% at $T{=}0.7$) than SciERC (60.3\% at $T{=}1.0$), directly contradicting the thinking-token hypothesis.

\section{Log-Probability Score Compression}\label{app:logprob_ties}

Under constrained decoding, log-probability scores are severely compressed within instances, limiting per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}, Figure~\ref{fig:lp_range_cdf}).
The median within-instance LP range is only 0.041 nats; we use $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ as an illustrative threshold to characterize this compression.
At this cutpoint, 60.3\% of instances ($n{=}529$, excluding empty gold annotations) have a within-sample range below $\varepsilon$, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\Delta|{<}0.026$).
The CDF rises smoothly with no cliff or discontinuity (Figure~\ref{fig:lp_range_cdf}); compression is a pervasive regime rather than a bimodal split.
This compression is stable across seeds: seed${=}456$ yields median LP range${=}0.040$ nats and tied fraction${=}62.2\%$ (vs.\ seed${=}42$: $0.041$ nats, $60.3\%$).
Seed~456 uses a different subtask flag (joint vs.\ ner for seeds 42 and 123); the LP distributions are statistically indistinguishable (median LP: 8.37 vs.\ 8.20 nats; Mann--Whitney $p{=}0.55$); the subtask change does not affect compression.
For comparison, SJ has only 12.5\% tied instances at the same threshold; SJ's advantage over LP for selection is one of score resolution, not information content.

The NER pattern reveals two complementary failure modes rather than a monotonic relationship between consistency and selection gain:
\begin{itemize}

\section{Exploratory Extension to Relation Extraction}\label{app:re_extension}

We extend the NER evaluation to relation extraction (RE) on SciERC as an exploratory single-benchmark analysis.
RE produces sets of (head, relation, tail) triples with partial overlap; 40\% of RE instances receive zero F1, and entity span errors account for 55.5\% of RE false negatives, a prerequisite failure that consistency signals cannot detect (\S\ref{app:additional}).
All RE results use Qwen3-8B unless noted; single-seed ($\text{seed}{=}42$) for $N{=}8$ analyses, 3-seed for $N{=}16$.

\paragraph{Quality estimation.}
RE quality estimation is reported in Table~\ref{tab:multiseed} (3-seed means).
The signal ranking differs from NER: VC leads ($\rho{=}0.309{\pm}0.024$), but LP rises to \#2 ($\rho{=}0.297{\pm}0.022$), above FK, SJ, and EM, a reversal reflecting RE's higher sensitivity to per-sample scoring.
RE miscalibration is more severe than NER (ECE 0.109--0.339; Figure~\ref{fig:reliability}).

\paragraph{Selection.}
Table~\ref{tab:re_cond_selection} presents RE selection at $N{=}8$: no signal outperforms single-sample (0.404) on the full set ($n{=}397$) or the non-zero subset ($n{=}238$), with 18.1~pp of unrealized oracle headroom.
At $N{=}16$ (Qwen3-4B, Table~\ref{tab:re_n16_selection}), LP is the sole positive signal ($\Delta{=}{+}0.7$~pp, $p{=}0.058$), consistent with LP being the strongest RE selection signal across scales.

\paragraph{Scale ablation.}
At 4B scale (Qwen3-4B, $N{=}8$, $\text{seed}{=}42$), RE quality estimation shows FK $\rho{=}0.359$ and LP $\rho{=}0.351$, both above their 8B counterparts (FK 0.275, LP 0.266), while SJ declines ($0.267$ vs.\ $0.250$).
Selection remains below single-sample on RE ($\Delta$ up to $-3.4$~pp) despite 17.1~pp of oracle headroom.

\paragraph{Free-form decoding.}
RE LP selection consistently reverses direction under free-form decoding ($+1.8{\pm}0.1$~pp across 4 seeds vs.\ $-0.9$~pp under constrained decoding at 8B; \S\ref{app:freeform_ablation}); constrained decoding's fixed template likely obscures LP signal in RE (\S\ref{app:mbr_discussion}).

Of $n{=}397$ RE instances, 238 (60\%) have non-zero F1 and 159 (40\%) have zero F1.

\section{MBR Decoding and Task-Specific Interactions}\label{app:mbr_discussion}

\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here: despite positive within-instance utility--F1 correlation, selection gains are limited by instance degeneracy, the core of the correlation-selection gap.
\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs, consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.

\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); whether the RE reversal replicates across seeds and generalizes to other RE benchmarks warrants further investigation.
The non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472: 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, and the newly non-tied subset shows a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.
Despite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible. Score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.
Free-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\rho$: 0.379$\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.

\section{LP Selection Failure Stability}\label{app:lp_failure_stability}

We analyze RE LP selection failures across three random seeds (constrained decoding, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, Qwen3-8B) to assess whether failures are systematic or stochastic.

\paragraph{Pairwise overlap.}
LP selection failures (instances where LP-selected F1 $<$ single-sample F1) show moderate cross-seed stability: the average pairwise Jaccard similarity is 0.42 (range: 0.38--0.46); failures are partially systematic (driven by instance complexity) but not fully deterministic.
The 3-way intersection contains 34 instances (27.9\% of any-seed failures), which constitutes a stable failure core.

\paragraph{Instance complexity drives failure.}
Table~\ref{tab:stable_failures} stratifies instances by failure stability.
Stable failures (all 3 seeds) involve more gold relations (2.12 vs.\ 1.62 for never-fail instances) and higher single-sample F1 (0.688 vs.\ 0.429); LP mis-selects on instances where the model already performs well, precisely the instances where selection would be most valuable.
Failure rate increases monotonically with gold relation count: 4.3\% at 1 relation, 20.7\% at 3 relations, 26.2\% at 6 relations.

docs/paper/sections/introduction.tex:8:Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we provide the first systematic empirical characterization of \textit{when and why} LP-based selection succeeds or fails for structured prediction, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.
docs/paper/sections/introduction.tex:13:For selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) in settings where both low instance degeneracy and adequate alignment are present, with gains scaling with $N$.
docs/paper/sections/introduction.tex:15:Three factors qualitatively shape this gap: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy} (13\textendash 87\% across our benchmarks) compresses the candidate space; (b)~\textit{oracle headroom} bounds the achievable gain; (c)~\textit{LP-quality alignment} (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) determines whether LP can discriminate candidates in non-degenerate instances (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
docs/paper/sections/introduction.tex:16:Our diagnosis is complementary to minimum Bayes risk (MBR) utility misalignment \cite{eikema2025structured}: where MBR failures in structured prediction stem from poorly chosen utility functions, we find that degeneracy eliminates candidate diversity before utility alignment matters.
docs/paper/sections/introduction.tex:17:Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates positively with F1 ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
docs/paper/sections/introduction.tex:18:Both mechanisms intensify with model capability: degeneracy rises with scale and training convergence (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). This creates a tension between model quality and test-time improvability.

1037	\paragraph{$N$-scaling: selection headroom vs.\ selection gain.}
1038	Table~\ref{tab:n_scaling_selection} traces the effect of sample count on degeneracy, oracle headroom, and per-signal selection gain.
1039	Oracle headroom grows roughly linearly with $N$ ($+4.4$~pp at $N{=}2$ to $+20.0$~pp at $N{=}32$).
1040	LP selection improves monotonically with $N$ ($+0.39$~pp at $N{=}8$ to $+0.95$~pp at $N{=}32$), but even at $N{=}32$, where degeneracy falls to 4\% and oracle headroom reaches ${\sim}20$~pp, the best signal captures less than 5\% of the available improvement.
1041	Degeneracy drops monotonically (43\% at $N{=}2$ to 4\% at $N{=}32$), yet reduced degeneracy does not unlock selection, consistent with the LoRA-rank ablation finding (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}).
1042	VC selection degrades with increasing $N$ ($-2.66$~pp at $N{=}2$ to $-4.35$~pp at $N{=}32$), consistent with mode-seeking bias in voting-based selection as the candidate pool grows.

1110	Oracle headroom increases monotonically with temperature ($+9.1$~pp at $T{=}0.5$ to $+14.6$~pp at $T{=}1.2$), confirming that higher temperature consistently expands the oracle ceiling under constrained structured decoding.
1111	Structural QE signals improve with temperature: SJ $\rho$ rises from $0.297$ ($T{=}0.5$) to $0.377$ ($T{=}1.2$), consistent with more diverse outputs providing richer pairwise evidence.

1117	\paragraph{Temperature controls degeneracy and LP spread.}
1118	Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy} reports instance degeneracy (constant F1, gold-filtered) and median within-instance LP range across four temperatures on SciERC.
1119	Both quantities are strictly monotonic in $T$: degeneracy falls from 41.4\% ($T{=}0.5$) to 14.9\% ($T{=}1.2$), while LP range increases from 0.015 to 0.058 nats.
1120	Temperature thus provides a direct lever for practitioners to shift the degeneracy regime.
1121	However, even at $T{=}1.2$ where degeneracy (14.9\%) approaches Few-NERD levels (${\sim}$13\%), within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ remains at 0.225, far below Few-NERD's ${\sim}$0.5.
1122	This confirms that temperature controls degeneracy but cannot improve LP-quality alignment, which is largely determined by task structure and remains relatively stable across generation configurations (\S\ref{app:epoch_confound}). LP-quality alignment, not degeneracy, is the primary predictor of LP selection direction (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

1165	\paragraph{Wider-to-narrower schema transfer.}
1166	When the SciERC-trained model (6 NER types) is applied to CoNLL (4 types), all signals remain significant ($p{<}0.001$) and structural signals improve over their in-domain levels (same model, seed${=}42$, $N{=}8$; in-domain $\rho$ from Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): VC reaches $\rho{=}0.469$ (in-domain $0.379$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.090$), SJ $\rho{=}0.378$ (in-domain $0.360$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.018$), and FK $\rho{=}0.285$ (in-domain $0.267$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.018$).
1167	The wider training schema subsumes CoNLL's narrower schema, so the model produces reasonable outputs even out-of-domain (single-sample F1${=}0.522$), and structural signals benefit from the simpler target schema's reduced output ambiguity.
1168	
1169	\paragraph{Narrower-to-wider schema transfer (excluded).}
1170	The reverse direction is excluded from our conclusions due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure.
1171	The CoNLL-trained model recognizes only 4 news entity types (PER, ORG, LOC, MISC) and has no relation extraction capability; when applied to SciERC's 6 scientific entity types and 7 relation types, the model cannot produce meaningful structured outputs (single-sample NER F1${=}0.009$, RE F1${=}0.001$).
1172	Under this regime, most signals flip to negative or near-zero correlations (Table~\ref{tab:ood}); only VC retains weak positive correlation ($\rho{=}0.105$, $p{=}0.016$).
1173	These negative correlations reflect the model systematically generating confident but incorrect outputs, a capability failure analogous to WNUT-17 (\S\ref{sec:qe_results}) and not evidence against signal utility.
1174	
1175	\paragraph{Asymmetry interpretation.}
1176	The directional asymmetry is driven by schema coverage: wider$\to$narrower preserves signal utility because the SciERC model's 6-type schema subsumes CoNLL's 4 types, while narrower$\to$wider fails because the CoNLL model lacks the entity and relation types required by SciERC.
1177	This extends the capability boundary identified on WNUT-17 to the domain-shift setting: confidence signals require sufficient model capability as a prerequisite, and results from the CoNLL$\to$SciERC direction should not be interpreted as evidence of signal degradation under domain shift.

1206	\paragraph{Severe overconfidence.}
1207	VerbConf exhibits extreme score compression: mean confidence is 8.58/10 on SciERC (single-sample F1${=}0.645$) and 9.24/10 on CoNLL (single-sample F1${=}0.904$), with most scores concentrated in the 8--10 range.
1208	This compression is more severe than LP (which spans a 0.041-nat median range); score compression is a general property of model self-assessment, not an artifact of log-probability computation.
1209	
1210	\paragraph{QE--selection decoupling.}
1211	VerbConf achieves higher $\rho$ than LP on both datasets (SciERC: 0.297 vs.\ 0.205; CoNLL: 0.337 vs.\ 0.316) and competitive AUROC (SciERC: 0.681 vs.\ 0.578; CoNLL: 0.747 vs.\ 0.753), yet yields the worst selection among all signals ($\Delta{=}{-}2.45$~pp on SciERC, $-1.93$~pp on CoNLL).
1212	This dissociation further demonstrates the correlation-selection gap: a signal can rank instances by expected quality without being able to discriminate candidates within an instance.
1213	The AUROC--$\rho$ decoupling on CoNLL (LP leads AUROC at 0.753 while VerbConf leads $\rho$ at 0.337) reflects differing sensitivity to binary vs.\ ordinal discrimination.

1276	\section{Per-Entity-Type LP Selection Analysis}\label{app:per_type_lp}
1277	
1278	Table~\ref{tab:per_type_lp} stratifies LP selection by entity type on Few-NERD, sorted by degeneracy rate.
1279	The degeneracy-gating mechanism holds at entity-type granularity: 7 of 8 types show positive LP selection gains, and the sole negative type (Art, $-0.17$~pp) has the highest degeneracy (19.8\%).
1280	The correlation between per-type degeneracy and oracle headroom is strong and significant (Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.881$, $p{=}0.004$; exact permutation $p{=}0.005$); degeneracy directly constrains the headroom available for selection.
