1346	\section{Calibration Baseline}\label{app:calibration_baseline}
1347	
1348	Standard calibration methods are monotonic transforms of log-probability and therefore preserve within-instance sample rankings: Platt scaling \cite{platt1999probabilistic} fits a logistic regression $\sigma(a \cdot \text{LP} + b)$, and temperature scaling \cite{guo2017calibration} divides logits by a scalar $\tau$.
1349	Since both preserve the argmax, selection F1 is identical to raw LP on all three datasets (Table~\ref{tab:calibration}).
1350	
1351	To break monotonicity, we fit a multi-feature Platt model (MF-Platt) using LP, token count, and entity count as inputs, trained on a held-out calibration split (20\% of the test set, 5-fold cross-validation on the remainder).
1352	MF-Platt can reorder candidates within an instance, yet yields no significant selection improvement: $\Delta{=}{-}1.1$~pp on SciERC ($p{=}0.72$), $+0.3$~pp on CoNLL ($p{=}0.31$), and $-0.6$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{=}0.83$).
1353	Platt scaling substantially improves probability calibration (ECE drops from 0.26--0.39 to 0.01--0.08), but better-calibrated probabilities do not translate to better selection.
1354	This parallels the supervised signal combination result (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}): neither stronger aggregation nor additional features can compensate for weak per-sample discriminative signal.

1374	\section{Epoch Confound Analysis}\label{app:epoch_confound}
1375	
1376	\paragraph{Training convergence modulates degeneracy.}
1377	Table~\ref{tab:epoch_confound} compares the 3-epoch model (used throughout the main text) with a 5-epoch variant on Few-NERD (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).
1378	Extended training increases greedy F1 by $+2.95$~pp (0.748 $\to$ 0.777) but nearly triples instance degeneracy (11.1\% $\to$ 31.3\%), reducing the fraction of instances with non-degenerate outputs from 85.6\% to 68.7\%.
1379	LP selection gains drop correspondingly ($+1.37$~pp $\to$ $+0.62$~pp), consistent with the degeneracy-gating mechanism identified in the main text (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
1380	Within-instance LP-quality alignment is relatively stable under this convergence shift (mean $\rho$: $0.524 \to 0.407$; median $\rho$: $0.667 \to 0.615$), consistent with alignment being determined primarily by task structure rather than training duration.
1381	
1382	Evaluation loss increases after epoch 3 (0.032 $\to$ 0.041 at epoch 5), and the best checkpoint by validation loss occurs at step 32{,}000 (approximately epoch 3.9).
1383	Standard early stopping practice thus naturally selects the low-degeneracy regime where LP selection is most effective.
1384	This finding refines the narrative: degeneracy is not a fixed property of datasets but is modulated by the degree of training convergence. Over-trained models compress their output distributions, collapsing diversity even on datasets that support it under well-regularized training.

1440	\subsection{Degeneracy-Aware LP Selection}\label{app:dals}
1441	
1442	The non-tied subset analysis (Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}) identifies within-instance LP range (max minus min LP across $N$ samples) as a per-instance degeneracy proxy: instances with near-zero LP range carry no discriminative signal.
1443	Degeneracy-aware LP selection (DALS) operationalizes this: when LP range exceeds $\tau{=}0.05$ (the threshold independently motivated by the non-tied analysis; Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}), select the highest-LP sample; otherwise fall back to greedy.
1444	On SciERC, DALS yields $+0.71{\pm}0.48$~pp (3-seed mean; individual seeds: $+0.19$ to $+1.14$~pp); on Few-NERD, $+0.30$~pp ($p{<}0.001$; gain remains positive across $\tau \in [0.01, 0.15]$); on CoNLL, where pure LP selection degrades F1 ($-0.85$~pp), DALS shows comparable degradation (Qwen: $-0.87$~pp; LLaMA: neutral).
1445	DALS improves over pure LP selection when degeneracy is moderate, provides partial damage control when LP selection is harmful, and defaults to greedy when LP range signals no information.
1446	While gains are modest and seed-sensitive, LP range serves as an operationally accessible degeneracy proxy, though the mixed cross-dataset results confirm that degeneracy gating alone cannot ensure positive selection outcomes.
1447	
1448	\paragraph{LOO $\tau$ sensitivity.}
1449	Leave-one-out (LOO) cross-validation across datasets reveals that the optimal $\tau$ spans two orders of magnitude: $\tau^*{=}0.001$ on Few-NERD, $0.05$ on SciERC, and $0.10$ on CoNLL.
1450	LOO regret (the gap between oracle and LOO-selected $\tau$) ranges from 0.51 to 1.21~pp.
1451	The best single cross-dataset $\tau$ ($\tau{=}0.05$) matches the independently motivated non-tied threshold, but yields dataset-specific suboptimality: even with oracle $\tau$, CoNLL remains at $-0.31$~pp.
1452	This sensitivity reinforces the diagnostic framing of DALS: per-dataset $\tau$ tuning is required for positive gains, and even optimally tuned DALS cannot overcome weak LP-quality alignment on high-degeneracy datasets.

\paragraph{$N$-scaling: selection headroom vs.\ selection gain.}
Table~\ref{tab:n_scaling_selection} traces the effect of sample count on degeneracy, oracle headroom, and per-signal selection gain.
Oracle headroom grows roughly linearly with $N$ ($+4.4$~pp at $N{=}2$ to $+20.0$~pp at $N{=}32$).
LP selection improves monotonically with $N$ ($+0.39$~pp at $N{=}8$ to $+0.95$~pp at $N{=}32$), but even at $N{=}32$, where degeneracy falls to 4\% and oracle headroom reaches ${\sim}20$~pp, the best signal captures less than 5\% of the available improvement.
Degeneracy drops monotonically (43\% at $N{=}2$ to 4\% at $N{=}32$), yet reduced degeneracy does not unlock selection, consistent with the LoRA-rank ablation finding (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}).
VC selection degrades with increasing $N$ ($-2.66$~pp at $N{=}2$ to $-4.35$~pp at $N{=}32$), consistent with mode-seeking bias in voting-based selection as the candidate pool grows.

\paragraph{Narrower-to-wider schema transfer (excluded).}
The reverse direction is excluded from our conclusions due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure.
The CoNLL-trained model recognizes only 4 news entity types (PER, ORG, LOC, MISC) and has no relation extraction capability; when applied to SciERC's 6 scientific entity types and 7 relation types, the model cannot produce meaningful structured outputs (single-sample NER F1${=}0.009$, RE F1${=}0.001$).

These negative correlations reflect the model systematically generating confident but incorrect outputs, a capability failure analogous to WNUT-17 (\S\ref{sec:qe_results}) and not evidence against signal utility.

\paragraph{Asymmetry interpretation.}
The directional asymmetry is driven by schema coverage: wider$\to$narrower preserves signal utility because the SciERC model's 6-type schema subsumes CoNLL's 4 types, while narrower$\to$wider fails because the CoNLL model lacks the entity and relation types required by SciERC.
This extends the capability boundary identified on WNUT-17 to the domain-shift setting: confidence signals require sufficient model capability as a prerequisite, and results from the CoNLL$\to$SciERC direction should not be interpreted as evidence of signal degradation under domain shift.

\section{Calibration Baseline}\label{app:calibration_baseline}

Standard calibration methods are monotonic transforms of log-probability and therefore preserve within-instance sample rankings: Platt scaling \cite{platt1999probabilistic} fits a logistic regression $\sigma(a \cdot \text{LP} + b)$, and temperature scaling \cite{guo2017calibration} divides logits by a scalar $\tau$.
Since both preserve the argmax, selection F1 is identical to raw LP on all three datasets (Table~\ref{tab:calibration}).

To break monotonicity, we fit a multi-feature Platt model (MF-Platt) using LP, token count, and entity count as inputs, trained on a held-out calibration split (20\% of the test set, 5-fold cross-validation on the remainder).
MF-Platt can reorder candidates within an instance, yet yields no significant selection improvement: $\Delta{=}{-}1.1$~pp on SciERC ($p{=}0.72$), $+0.3$~pp on CoNLL ($p{=}0.31$), and $-0.6$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{=}0.83$).
Platt scaling substantially improves probability calibration (ECE drops from 0.26--0.39 to 0.01--0.08), but better-calibrated probabilities do not translate to better selection.
This parallels the supervised signal combination result (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}): neither stronger aggregation nor additional features can compensate for weak per-sample discriminative signal.

\section{Epoch Confound Analysis}\label{app:epoch_confound}

\paragraph{Training convergence modulates degeneracy.}
Table~\ref{tab:epoch_confound} compares the 3-epoch model (used throughout the main text) with a 5-epoch variant on Few-NERD (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).
Extended training increases greedy F1 by $+2.95$~pp (0.748 $\to$ 0.777) but nearly triples instance degeneracy (11.1\% $\to$ 31.3\%), reducing the fraction of instances with non-degenerate outputs from 85.6\% to 68.7\%.
LP selection gains drop correspondingly ($+1.37$~pp $\to$ $+0.62$~pp), consistent with the degeneracy-gating mechanism identified in the main text (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Within-instance LP-quality alignment is relatively stable under this convergence shift (mean $\rho$: $0.524 \to 0.407$; median $\rho$: $0.667 \to 0.615$), consistent with alignment being determined primarily by task structure rather than training duration.

Evaluation loss increases after epoch 3 (0.032 $\to$ 0.041 at epoch 5), and the best checkpoint by validation loss occurs at step 32{,}000 (approximately epoch 3.9).
Standard early stopping practice thus naturally selects the low-degeneracy regime where LP selection is most effective.
This finding refines the narrative: degeneracy is not a fixed property of datasets but is modulated by the degree of training convergence. Over-trained models compress their output distributions, collapsing diversity even on datasets that support it under well-regularized training.

\paragraph{SciERC epoch curve.}
Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc} extends the analysis to SciERC with a 3-point curve (3, 5, 10 epochs; Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).
Degeneracy increases monotonically (6.4\% $\to$ 17.8\% $\to$ 47.8\%), and within-instance LP-quality correlation degrades in tandem (median $\rho$: 0.319 $\to$ 0.262 $\to$ 0.112; mean $\rho$: 0.273 $\to$ 0.179 $\to$ 0.066), confirming that overtraining erodes both diversity and LP alignment simultaneously.
The fraction of instances with positive LP-quality correlation also declines (76.4\% at 3 epochs $\to$ 64.1\% at 5 epochs $\to$ 54.0\% at 10 epochs).
LP selection does not yield significant gains at any training duration ($-1.24$, $+0.64$, $+1.02$~pp; all below the ${\approx}$1.5~pp MDE), despite oracle headroom ranging from 8.4 to 15.0~pp.
The 3-epoch model has higher within-instance alignment ($\rho{=}0.319$) than the 5-epoch model ($\rho{=}0.262$), yet LP selection is worse ($-1.24$ vs.\ $+0.64$~pp): at 6.4\% degeneracy, more non-degenerate instances enter the candidate pool, but LP ranking precision is too low to exploit them, so the broader pool hurts rather than helps. This illustrates that low degeneracy does not ensure selection gains; LP-quality alignment determines selection direction.
At 10 epochs, the model retains competitive greedy F1 (0.649 vs.\ 0.650 at 3 epochs) yet conditions are unfavorable: 47.8\% degenerate instances and $\rho{=}0.112$.
The gradient confirms that degeneracy is convergence-driven rather than a fixed dataset property: extended training compresses output distributions, degrading both diversity and within-instance alignment. However, the epoch-to-epoch alignment variation ($\Delta\rho_{\text{median}}{=}0.057$) is small relative to the cross-dataset gap (SciERC ${\sim}$0.3 vs.\ Few-NERD ${\sim}$0.5), consistent with alignment being primarily dataset-intrinsic: training convergence modulates alignment at the margin but cannot shift a dataset into the strong-alignment regime.
Even at the most favorable epoch (3-epoch, $\rho{=}0.319$), SciERC alignment remains below the ${\sim}$0.5 threshold associated with successful LP selection on Few-NERD.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
The Few-NERD epoch analysis covers 2 points (3 vs.\ 5 epochs); the SciERC curve provides a 3-point gradient showing monotonic degeneracy increase with simultaneous within-instance alignment degradation.
CoNLL epoch variation remains unverified; high-degeneracy datasets (CoNLL at 59--89\%) may exhibit a ceiling effect where additional training has limited marginal impact.
All Few-NERD results in the main text use the 3-epoch model (standard early stopping); the 5-epoch comparison is a controlled ablation.
All SciERC results use the 5-epoch model; the 3- and 10-epoch variants serve as controlled ablations.

\subsection{Degeneracy-Aware LP Selection}\label{app:dals}

The non-tied subset analysis (Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}) identifies within-instance LP range (max minus min LP across $N$ samples) as a per-instance degeneracy proxy: instances with near-zero LP range carry no discriminative signal.
Degeneracy-aware LP selection (DALS) operationalizes this: when LP range exceeds $\tau{=}0.05$ (the threshold independently motivated by the non-tied analysis; Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}), select the highest-LP sample; otherwise fall back to greedy.
On SciERC, DALS yields $+0.71{\pm}0.48$~pp (3-seed mean; individual seeds: $+0.19$ to $+1.14$~pp); on Few-NERD, $+0.30$~pp ($p{<}0.001$; gain remains positive across $\tau \in [0.01, 0.15]$); on CoNLL, where pure LP selection degrades F1 ($-0.85$~pp), DALS shows comparable degradation (Qwen: $-0.87$~pp; LLaMA: neutral).
DALS improves over pure LP selection when degeneracy is moderate, provides partial damage control when LP selection is harmful, and defaults to greedy when LP range signals no information.
While gains are modest and seed-sensitive, LP range serves as an operationally accessible degeneracy proxy, though the mixed cross-dataset results confirm that degeneracy gating alone cannot ensure positive selection outcomes.

\paragraph{LOO $\tau$ sensitivity.}
Leave-one-out (LOO) cross-validation across datasets reveals that the optimal $\tau$ spans two orders of magnitude: $\tau^*{=}0.001$ on Few-NERD, $0.05$ on SciERC, and $0.10$ on CoNLL.
LOO regret (the gap between oracle and LOO-selected $\tau$) ranges from 0.51 to 1.21~pp.
The best single cross-dataset $\tau$ ($\tau{=}0.05$) matches the independently motivated non-tied threshold, but yields dataset-specific suboptimality: even with oracle $\tau$, CoNLL remains at $-0.31$~pp.
This sensitivity reinforces the diagnostic framing of DALS: per-dataset $\tau$ tuning is required for positive gains, and even optimally tuned DALS cannot overcome weak LP-quality alignment on high-degeneracy datasets.

\subsection{Conditional Decomposition of LP Selection}\label{app:conditional_decomp}

To test whether LP-quality alignment drives selection gains within datasets, we restrict LP selection to the favorable subset: non-degenerate instances whose within-instance LP range exceeds the dataset-specific median (SciERC: 0.040 nats, CoNLL: 0.062, Few-NERD: 0.067).
Table~\ref{tab:conditional_decomp} reports results across three datasets.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{LP selection on the favorable subset (non-degenerate instances with LP range above the dataset-specific median) per dataset (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). CI: bootstrap 95\% confidence interval.}
\label{tab:conditional_decomp}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
Dataset & LP $\Delta$ (pp) & 95\% CI & Interpretation \\
\midrule
SciERC & $+$2.47 & [$+$0.30, $+$4.70] & significant positive \\
Few-NERD & $+$0.63 & [$-$0.02, $+$1.30] & marginal positive \\
CoNLL & $-$1.78 & [$-$2.83, $-$0.76] & significant negative \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

On SciERC, restricting to the favorable subset recovers a significant LP gain, consistent with LP-quality alignment driving selection within the non-degenerate pool.
On Few-NERD, the trend is directionally consistent but the confidence interval crosses zero; the full-dataset result ($+1.39$~pp, $p{<}0.001$) reflects the larger sample size rather than a stronger per-instance effect.
CoNLL remains negative even on the favorable subset, consistent with the ceiling-regime interpretation: at $>$90\% greedy F1, residual errors are idiosyncratic and LP cannot rank corrections.

\subsection{Entity-Token LP Decomposition}\label{app:entity_token_lp}

Full-sequence LP averages over all output tokens, diluting entity-relevant signal with formatting and schema tokens.
Entity-token LP restricts the average to tokens within entity text and type spans, yielding $4{\times}$ higher within-instance variance (median 0.000644 vs.\ 0.000161).
Table~\ref{tab:entity_token_lp} compares the two aggregation strategies on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).

\subsection{Entity-Level Majority Voting}\label{app:entity_merge}

Entity-level majority voting constructs a merged output by including all (text, type) entity tuples that appear in at least $k$ of $N$ samples (with $k = N/2$ as the default majority threshold).

docs/paper/sections/related_work.tex:7:All target discrete-answer reasoning; structured prediction requires different gating signals because degeneracy operates at the entity-set level.
docs/paper/sections/related_work.tex:10:\citet{yao2026consistency} show consistency correlates with accuracy for LLM-based NER/RE; we show correlation alone does not ensure selection gains, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as blocking mechanisms.
docs/paper/sections/related_work.tex:21:Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid}; unlike MT where MBR yields consistent gains \cite{freitag2022high} and code generation where execution-based MBR improves selection \cite{shi2022mbr}, instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom MBR needs even when utility is well-aligned ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
docs/paper/sections/related_work.tex:22:\citet{eikema2025structured} find MBR utilities degrade on structured outputs; our diagnosis is complementary: degeneracy, not utility misalignment, is the primary bottleneck.
docs/paper/sections/introduction.tex:8:Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we provide the first systematic empirical characterization of \textit{when and why} LP-based selection succeeds or fails for structured prediction, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.
docs/paper/sections/introduction.tex:13:For selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) in settings where both low instance degeneracy and adequate alignment are present, with gains scaling with $N$.
docs/paper/sections/introduction.tex:15:Three factors qualitatively shape this gap: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy} (13\textendash 87\% across our benchmarks) compresses the candidate space; (b)~\textit{oracle headroom} bounds the achievable gain; (c)~\textit{LP-quality alignment} (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) determines whether LP can discriminate candidates in non-degenerate instances (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
docs/paper/sections/introduction.tex:16:Our diagnosis is complementary to minimum Bayes risk (MBR) utility misalignment \cite{eikema2025structured}: where MBR failures in structured prediction stem from poorly chosen utility functions, we find that degeneracy eliminates candidate diversity before utility alignment matters.
docs/paper/sections/introduction.tex:17:Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates positively with F1 ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
docs/paper/sections/introduction.tex:18:Both mechanisms intensify with model capability: degeneracy rises with scale and training convergence (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). This creates a tension between model quality and test-time improvability.

docs/paper/sections/introduction.tex:27:We evaluate five signals from three families (structural, surface, and model-internal) on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc} as a primary medium-difficulty test bed, with Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (low-degeneracy contrast), CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (ceiling-effect control), and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (signal-collapse boundary), using two 8B models (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with a 4B ablation (Qwen3-4B).
docs/paper/sections/introduction.tex:38:    Instance degeneracy causally modulates LP within fixed settings (epoch and temperature ablations), but does not predict cross-dataset direction ($\rho{=}0.052$, 23 configurations); structural signals fail by construction; supervised combinations and hidden state probes (Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}) confirm the gap persists.

docs/paper/sections/method.tex:61:We define \textbf{instance degeneracy} as the fraction of instances where all $N$ samples yield identical F1;\footnote{``Identical F1'' means constant F1 across all $N$ samples for a given instance, not necessarily F1${=}1.0$. Samples may differ in surface form but produce the same entity set and thus the same score.} for these instances, no signal can improve selection.
docs/paper/sections/abstract.tex:6:We identify three qualitative factors: instance degeneracy, oracle headroom, and LP-quality alignment; the gap persists at 72B zero-shot scale, confirming it is a structural property of the task rather than a fine-tuning artifact.
docs/paper/sections/abstract.tex:7:The diagnostic naturally motivates entity-level \textit{construction}, adapting entity voting to stochastic sampling: LP-weighted aggregation improves F1 by $+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD and $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC (multi-seed mean, $p{<}0.005$). Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment.

\begin{abstract}
Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists.
We evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation (QE) and sample selection on four NER benchmarks across fine-tuned 4B\textendash 8B and zero-shot 72B models.
All signals achieve reliable QE ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL-2003, area under the ROC curve [AUROC] up to 0.82), enabling selective prediction ($+5$--$8$\,pp F1 at 80\% coverage).
For instance-level selection, log-probability (LP) succeeds only where LP-quality alignment is strong, and gains are absent elsewhere despite large oracle headroom (the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}).
We identify three qualitative factors: instance degeneracy, oracle headroom, and LP-quality alignment; the gap persists at 72B zero-shot scale, confirming it is a structural property of the task rather than a fine-tuning artifact.
The diagnostic naturally motivates entity-level \textit{construction}, adapting entity voting to stochastic sampling: LP-weighted aggregation improves F1 by $+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD and $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC (multi-seed mean, $p{<}0.005$). Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment.
\end{abstract}

1	\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
2	
3	\paragraph{Self-consistency and test-time scaling.}
4	Self-consistency \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} improves reasoning via majority voting; extensions handle free-form text \cite{chen2024usc, thirukovalluru2024atomic, manakul2023selfcheckgpt}.
5	Test-time scaling studies \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys} and reward-free selectors \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty, wang2025rankedvoting, oh2026latentsc} rely on answer-level agreement.
6	Adaptive variants gate on answer agreement \cite{aggarwal2023adaptive}, input difficulty \cite{wang2025make, feng2025optimal}, or response confidence \cite{kim2026reasc}; \citet{chen2025twofailures} diagnose SC failure modes without proposing gating.
7	All target discrete-answer reasoning; structured prediction requires different gating signals because degeneracy operates at the entity-set level.
8	
9	\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
10	\citet{yao2026consistency} show consistency correlates with accuracy for LLM-based NER/RE; we show correlation alone does not ensure selection gains, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as blocking mechanisms.
11	CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses confidence with consistency; our supervised baseline confirms combination is not the bottleneck (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}).
12	Earlier work on confidence for structured prediction \cite{culotta2004confidence, mejer2010confidence, fomicheva2020unsupervised} establishes the paradigm we extend to set-valued outputs.
13	Ensemble approaches aggregate predictions from multiple models or prompts \cite{florian2003named, xiao2025el4ner}; \citet{xie2023zeroshot} propose two-stage entity voting for zero-shot NER, the closest prior work to our entity-level construction.
14	LLM-Blender \cite{jiang2023llmblender} fuses outputs from multiple LLMs via pairwise ranking, whereas our single-model stochastic sampling derives diversity from temperature rather than model heterogeneity.
15	Our entity-level construction aggregates across samples from a single fine-tuned model, without requiring model diversity or prompt engineering.
16	Our evaluation builds on generative IE \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie, li2023codeie, wadhwa2023revisiting, xie2024selfimproving} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided, dong2024xgrammar, park2024grammar, schall2025hidden}.
17	\citet{yun2025price} show structured formats induce diversity collapse; our LP compression (median range 0.041 nats; \S\ref{sec:discussion}) corroborates this for NER.
18	
19	\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and MBR decoding.}
20	Surveys cover confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence}, uncertainty quantification \cite{xia2025survey}, and calibration \cite{hobelsberger2025systematic}; semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic, farquhar2024detecting} and P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} provide model-internal alternatives.
21	Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid}; unlike MT where MBR yields consistent gains \cite{freitag2022high} and code generation where execution-based MBR improves selection \cite{shi2022mbr}, instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom MBR needs even when utility is well-aligned ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).

23	Our QE results connect to selective prediction \cite{geifman2017selective, kuleshov2015calibrated, varshney2022investigating}: signals with AUROC up to 0.82 support abstention policies independent of sample selection.
24	
25	\paragraph{Best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers.}
26	\citet{gao2023scaling} establish BoN scaling laws and \citet{chen2021evaluating} define the pass@$k$ metric for code generation; our unsupervised signals face a more fundamental limitation than reward overoptimization.

29	Fine-tuning \cite{kirk2024understanding} and constrained decoding \cite{holtzman2020curious, vijayakumar2018diverse} both limit the diversity recoverable for selection.

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Self-consistency and test-time scaling.}
Self-consistency \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} improves reasoning via majority voting; extensions handle free-form text \cite{chen2024usc, thirukovalluru2024atomic, manakul2023selfcheckgpt}.
Test-time scaling studies \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys} and reward-free selectors \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty, wang2025rankedvoting, oh2026latentsc} rely on answer-level agreement.
Adaptive variants gate on answer agreement \cite{aggarwal2023adaptive}, input difficulty \cite{wang2025make, feng2025optimal}, or response confidence \cite{kim2026reasc}; \citet{chen2025twofailures} diagnose SC failure modes without proposing gating.
All target discrete-answer reasoning; structured prediction requires different gating signals because degeneracy operates at the entity-set level.

\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
\citet{yao2026consistency} show consistency correlates with accuracy for LLM-based NER/RE; we show correlation alone does not ensure selection gains, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as blocking mechanisms.
CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses confidence with consistency; our supervised baseline confirms combination is not the bottleneck (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}).
Earlier work on confidence for structured prediction \cite{culotta2004confidence, mejer2010confidence, fomicheva2020unsupervised} establishes the paradigm we extend to set-valued outputs.
Ensemble approaches aggregate predictions from multiple models or prompts \cite{florian2003named, xiao2025el4ner}; \citet{xie2023zeroshot} propose two-stage entity voting for zero-shot NER, the closest prior work to our entity-level construction.
LLM-Blender \cite{jiang2023llmblender} fuses outputs from multiple LLMs via pairwise ranking, whereas our single-model stochastic sampling derives diversity from temperature rather than model heterogeneity.
Our entity-level construction aggregates across samples from a single fine-tuned model, without requiring model diversity or prompt engineering.
Our evaluation builds on generative IE \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie, li2023codeie, wadhwa2023revisiting, xie2024selfimproving} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided, dong2024xgrammar, park2024grammar, schall2025hidden}.
\citet{yun2025price} show structured formats induce diversity collapse; our LP compression (median range 0.041 nats; \S\ref{sec:discussion}) corroborates this for NER.

\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and MBR decoding.}
Surveys cover confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence}, uncertainty quantification \cite{xia2025survey}, and calibration \cite{hobelsberger2025systematic}; semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic, farquhar2024detecting} and P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} provide model-internal alternatives.
Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid}; unlike MT where MBR yields consistent gains \cite{freitag2022high} and code generation where execution-based MBR improves selection \cite{shi2022mbr}, instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom MBR needs even when utility is well-aligned ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\citet{eikema2025structured} find MBR utilities degrade on structured outputs; our diagnosis is complementary: degeneracy, not utility misalignment, is the primary bottleneck.
Our QE results connect to selective prediction \cite{geifman2017selective, kuleshov2015calibrated, varshney2022investigating}: signals with AUROC up to 0.82 support abstention policies independent of sample selection.

\paragraph{Best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers.}
\citet{gao2023scaling} establish BoN scaling laws and \citet{chen2021evaluating} define the pass@$k$ metric for code generation; our unsupervised signals face a more fundamental limitation than reward overoptimization.
Trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify, fernandes2022quality} and self-evaluation guided search \cite{xie2023selfevaluation} learn per-sample scoring.
CISC \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc} and Self-Certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty} derive per-sample confidence from hidden states rather than output statistics, but require architecture-specific access to intermediate representations; these hidden-state signals remain untested for structured prediction (\S Limitations).
Fine-tuning \cite{kirk2024understanding} and constrained decoding \cite{holtzman2020curious, vijayakumar2018diverse} both limit the diversity recoverable for selection.

\paragraph{Cross-configuration selection analysis.}
Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection} extends the selection analysis to five additional configurations.
On LLaMA SciERC, where output diversity remains substantial (18\% identical outputs, 39\% unique), LP achieves the highest selection F1 (0.652) at $N{=}8$ but still falls within bootstrap noise of single-sample (0.646), replicating the gap observed on Qwen SciERC (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
On LLaMA FewNERD ($n{=}32{,}565$, 3-seed mean), LP is the only signal with positive selection ($+0.36$~pp), confirming LP as the most robust selection signal across model families (Qwen FewNERD: $+1.39$~pp, Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}). All structural signals degrade selection (VC $-2.39$~pp, SJ $-0.52$~pp), consistent with the Qwen pattern. LLaMA FewNERD degeneracy ($23.4{\pm}4.7$\%, 3 seeds) is higher than Qwen ($12.7$\%), illustrating the capability-diversity tension: LLaMA achieves stronger greedy F1 ($0.784$ vs.\ $0.748$, $+3.6$~pp) but at the cost of higher degeneracy ($+10.7$~pp) and reduced oracle headroom ($10.0$ vs.\ $12.4$~pp).
On CoNLL, 48--87\% of instances produce identical outputs across all $N$ samples; this reflects a ceiling effect (single-sample F1 ${\approx}$0.91--0.92) rather than signal failure, and selection analysis on these configurations is uninformative because there is little per-sample variance for any signal to exploit.

Our evaluation covers four NER datasets; an exploratory RE extension on SciERC is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension} but generalization to other RE benchmarks remains unvalidated.
All experiments use English-language datasets; cross-lingual generalization remains untested.
Entity-level construction assumes the model produces useful partial outputs across samples; when model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17, 51\% F1${=}0$), this precondition fails and construction cannot improve over greedy.
We cover 4B\textendash 8B fine-tuned and 72B zero-shot; the gap persists at 72B but behavior with closed-source APIs or 72B fine-tuning is untested.
Our supervised approaches (DeBERTa verifier, hidden state probes, MLP/RF on signal combinations) all fail to close the oracle gap; whether content-aware verifiers with access to task-specific structure could succeed remains open.

We evaluate at $N{=}8$ (primary) and $N{=}16$; behavior at larger sample sizes is unknown (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
The free-form ablation covers SciERC NER and CoNLL NER with one model; RE free-form results are in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint used empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks; a three-part analysis rules out this confound (Appendix~\ref{app:thinking_token}).
LP compression worsens on easy datasets at lower temperature (CoNLL tied fractions reach 95.8\% at $T{=}0.7$); whether reduced temperature translates to selection gains remains untested.
We tested verbalized confidence \cite{lin2022teaching, tian2023calibration} as a second per-sample signal; it exhibits severe overconfidence (mean 8.58/10 on SciERC, 9.24/10 on CoNLL) and yields the weakest QE and selection among all signals (Appendix~\ref{app:verbalized_confidence}).
Ad-hoc LP${\times}$VC combinations yield at most $+0.2$~pp over greedy (not significant; \S\ref{sec:discussion}); whether \textit{learned} combinations could close the gap remains open.
The $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold used for tied/non-tied LP stratification is a post-hoc exploratory choice; while selection F1 is stable across $\varepsilon \in [0, 0.2]$ (Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}), the specific subset gains should be interpreted as characterizing the compression phenomenon rather than as a tuned selection strategy.
We tested one remedy for LP compression (entity-token-only LP, excluding format/schema tokens) which fails to improve selection despite increasing within-instance variance on SciERC ($4{\times}$); LP${\times}$VC combinations also fail to recover selection (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). Our supervised signal combination baseline uses only the five unsupervised signals studied; a DeBERTa verifier encoding input-output pairs also fails to close the gap (preliminary, SciERC $n{=}106$), hidden state probes on the generating model's representations improve correlation ($+37$\% on SciERC) but do not improve selection (gap closure $-5.1$\%; Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}), ; the bottleneck extends to model-internal access. Entity embeddings and calibration-based approaches remain untested.
Other per-sample scoring methods exist but were not evaluated: Self-Certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty} (consistency of token-level self-evaluation) and P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} (model's own probability estimate of correctness) both produce per-sample scores and could in principle address the alignment bottleneck; whether they suffer from similar compression under fine-tuning is unknown.
Our selection experiments use 3 training seeds for Few-NERD and CoNLL (stability $\sigma{\leq}0.04$~pp for LP selection); these confirm robustness on the key positive and negative datasets. SciERC uses 1 primary seed with high seed sensitivity ($\sigma{=}0.48$~pp, $n{=}529$), which reflects limited within-seed statistical power.
Few-NERD models are trained for 3 epochs (vs.\ 5 for other datasets) due to earlier convergence; epoch confound analyses on both Few-NERD (2-point) and SciERC (3-point, including 10-epoch overfitting) are provided in Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}.
